title: I feel so alone
seoTitle: When You Feel So Alone: Loneliness, Faith, and What Helps
description: Feeling alone, even in a marriage or a crowded church? What the Bible says about loneliness, why it's so hard now, and small steps that help this week.
summary: Lonely in a crowd, a marriage, or a church? What Scripture says, why it's so hard now, and small steps that help this week.
askedAs: What does the Bible say about loneliness?
how to make friends as an adult
answer: You can be around people all week and still wonder who would notice if you went quiet for a month. Maybe your friends drifted into marriages, jobs, and other cities, or the person you shared your life with is gone. You might sit in a full church, or lie beside a spouse, and feel completely unknown. Loneliness is not a character flaw or a lack of faith. It's the ache of a person made for company who isn't getting enough of it, and God called that condition not good before anything in the world had gone wrong. Much of what makes it so hard isn't your doing, and small steps this week can begin to change it. If the loneliness has turned into thoughts of not wanting to be here, please reach someone tonight using the help below.
happening:
Loneliness is the gap between the connection you have and the connection you need, which isn't the same as being alone. Some people live alone and are content, and some are surrounded all day and feel unknown. It takes many shapes: the single adult whose friends married and disappeared into their own families, the widow whose phone went quiet a month after the funeral, the husband or wife lying beside someone who feels far away, the family that moved for a job and knows no one yet, the pastor who is known by everyone and known by no one. For many it's the person who comes to church every week, shakes hands at the greeting, and drives home without anyone learning their name. And some loneliness is imposed. If a spouse or partner controls who you see, or someone at home makes you afraid, that's a safety problem before it's a loneliness problem, and the National Domestic Violence Hotline, listed near the top of this page, can help you plan for your safety.

It tends to hurt most at particular hours, like Sunday afternoons or the moment you want to tell someone something and realize there's no one to tell. Many people feel it in their bodies too, in poor sleep and a low, constant tiredness. And loneliness feeds itself. The longer it lasts, the more guarded you become: you read a neutral face as rejection, you skip the gathering because you're sure you'll be awkward, and each small retreat makes the next reach harder. Underneath runs a quiet question: *what is wrong with me?*

The common explanations each hold part of the truth. The medical and psychological ones are right that loneliness affects body and mind, and that the cycle of withdrawal and suspicion can be broken with help. The spiritual one is right that some of the longing is for God; Augustine began his *Confessions* by telling God that our hearts are restless until they rest in him. But each, taken alone, leaves something out. The first two can make loneliness sound like a private malfunction, when it's also a sign that something in the way we live has gone wrong. And the spiritual one, told carelessly, contradicts God himself, who looked at the first man, with nothing standing between him and his Maker, and still called his aloneness not good.

Loneliness and despair can sit close together. If being alone has started to turn into thoughts that you don't want to be here, or that people would be better off without you, that is not a failure of faith, and it isn't something to wait out alone. Reach a person tonight through the lines at the top of this page. You don't have to be in danger to call, and you don't need the right words. The federal agency that funds 988 lists loneliness itself among the reasons people reach out.

scripture.intro: Scripture doesn't treat loneliness as a modern problem or a private embarrassment. It names loneliness in its second chapter and gives lonely people words to pray, and it shows both Jesus and Paul asking their friends to come near. Read slowly, these passages say your loneliness has been seen, and that God's answer to it has always included a people.

passages.text: The LORD God also said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper.”
passages.reading: This is the first time God calls anything in his creation not good, and it comes before anything has gone wrong. The man has a garden to tend and God himself for company, yet God says it isn't good for him to be alone, and then acts on it. So your need for people is not a spiritual failure. It's part of how you were made. Marriage is this chapter's answer and one of God's good answers to loneliness, but Scripture refuses to make it the only one: Jesus never married, and Paul wrote as an unmarried man (1 Corinthians 7:8), yet neither lived without friends.

passages.text: Look to my right and see; no one attends to me. There is no refuge for me; no one cares for my soul. I cry to You, O LORD: “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.” ... Free my soul from prison, that I may praise Your name. The righteous will gather around me because of Your goodness to me.
passages.reading: The heading sets this prayer in the cave, which points back to the years David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1; 24:3), and verse 6 still speaks of pursuers. In the Psalms the right hand is where a protector stands (Psalm 109:31), and David looks there and finds no one: "no one cares for my soul." But he doesn't keep that to himself. He says it to God, whom he calls his portion "in the land of the living," here and now, not only in heaven. And the psalm ends by expecting company: "The righteous will gather around me." He trusts that God's answer will include people, and you may ask for the same.

passages.text: He took with Him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee and began to be sorrowful and deeply distressed. Then He said to them, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch with Me.” ... Then Jesus returned to the disciples and found them sleeping. “Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?” He asked Peter.
passages.reading: On the night before he died, Jesus took his three closest friends deeper into the garden, told them how heavy his sorrow was, and asked them to stay awake with him. Though he was in perfect communion with his Father, he still wanted his friends near. They slept, and within hours "all the disciples deserted Him and fled" (Matthew 26:56). He knows from the inside what it is to be alone among friends, and Scripture calls him able "to sympathize with our weaknesses" (Hebrews 4:15). There's a hard word here too. Most of us have slept through someone else's Gethsemane, and he died for friends like us.

passages.text: Make every effort to come to me quickly, because Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. ... At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me ...
passages.reading: This letter presents itself as Paul's last, written in chains in Rome with his death close (2 Timothy 1:16-17; 4:6). One companion has left for love of the world, others have gone elsewhere, and at his hearing no one stood with him. Then the letter turns: "But the Lord stood by me." Yet the same letter asks Timothy to bring "the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas" (2 Timothy 4:13) and to "come to me before winter" (2 Timothy 4:21). He needed God, a friend, and a coat, and said so. The Lord stood by him, and he still asked for Timothy.

passages.text: A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation. God settles the lonely in families; He leads the prisoners out to prosperity, but the rebellious dwell in a sun-scorched land.
passages.reading: Psalm 68 is a loud processional hymn (Psalm 68:24-25), but early on the psalm pauses to say who this God is at home: a father to the fatherless, who settles the lonely in families. The Hebrew word behind families is the ordinary word for a house. God's answer to the solitary is a household, and in the New Testament that promise comes to rest in the church. Jesus promised those who had left their own families for him "houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children" in this life, "along with persecutions" (Mark 10:30). When a lonely person comes and goes from one of our churches unknown, we have failed to be what this psalm promised.

whyHard:
When you're lonely, the easiest explanation is that something is wrong with you. Habits do matter, and the steps below are about habits. But that's only part of the story, and usually the smaller part. Loneliness is also something that happened to a whole culture over most of a lifetime, and it helps to see it, because as long as you believe it's simply your fault, shame will keep you from doing much about it.

In his 2000 book *Bowling Alone*, the Harvard political scientist Robert Putnam documented how Americans, over the last decades of the twentieth century, drifted out of the ordinary associations that used to fill a week. The title came from one of his examples: people kept bowling, but fewer of them bowled in leagues. Clubs, lodges, unions, parent groups, card nights, dinner parties, and congregations had all produced friendship as a byproduct. Nobody had to set out to make friends; you saw the same people every Thursday for years and one day realized you had them. People still needed one another, but the places that did the introducing thinned out, and very little took their place.

Many of us also move for work or school, sometimes more than once, and each move cuts a few threads. Parents end up two states away, the neighbors are pleasant strangers, and college friends become photographs. Into that gap came the phone. It can carry a real friendship across a distance, but it's far better at the feeling of company than at the substance of it, and we reach for it at the very hour we most need a person. It gives us an evening of watching other people's lives without once being seen ourselves.

Beneath all of this sits a belief most of us absorbed without choosing it: that a mature person doesn't really need anyone. We say *I don't want to be a burden* as though needing people were a moral failure, so the lonely carry a second weight on top of the first, the shame of being lonely at all, and the shame keeps them quiet. We Christians have our own version. We rightly learned that faith must be personal and then quietly made it private, forgetting that most of the New Testament's letters were written to churches. When Paul wrote, "you yourselves are God's temple," every *you* in that sentence was plural in Greek (1 Corinthians 3:16).

And then there is the church, which was meant to be the answer and has too often become part of the problem. Gathered worship is the heart of a church's life, and there is real good in that Sunday hour. But many of our churches have organized nearly everything around it, a room where people face the same direction and then go home, and a person can attend faithfully for years without anyone learning their name. An audience cannot obey the commands to "carry one another's burdens" (Galatians 6:2) or to "weep with those who weep" (Romans 12:15). Pastors are tempted to count the room and call it a family, and I am a pastor. We built big rooms and too few tables, and then wondered why people who never missed a Sunday went home to empty kitchens.

None of this excuses any of us from the small, costly work of reaching toward one another. It does mean the shame is misplaced. If you're lonely, you're feeling in your own life the cost of a way of living we built together, and those of us in the church did too little to resist it. The ache is not proof that you're unlovable. It's proof that you were made for a household, and too many of us stopped building one.

thisWeek.intro: Loneliness rarely gives way to one big connection. It yields to small, repeated steps toward the same people over time. Pick one or two of these, start before you feel ready, and expect it to be awkward; awkward is what the beginning of friendship usually feels like.

steps.title: Say it to God in plain words
steps.body: Tell God the truth, out loud if you can. You're allowed to borrow David's prayer: "Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted" (Psalm 25:16). Then be specific about who you miss and which hour is hardest. Prayer won't replace the people you need, but it's where honesty begins, and honesty makes the other steps easier.

steps.title: Send one honest message
steps.body: Tomorrow, text or call one person you'd like to be closer to. Make it specific: *I've been thinking about you. Could we get coffee Saturday?* If you can, add one true sentence: *Honestly, I've been pretty lonely lately.* A specific invitation is easier to accept than a vague one, and one honest sentence can open more than a year of small talk.

steps.title: Go back to the same people every week
steps.body: Friendship mostly grows from seeing the same faces again and again without having to plan it. Pick something that meets weekly: the same service and pew, a small group, a choir, a serving team, or a grief or recovery group if that's what you're carrying. Working alongside people is often easier than sitting across from them. Learn one name, and give it two months before you judge it.

steps.title: Say yes to the next invitation
steps.body: Loneliness will talk you out of almost every invitation. Say yes to the next one anyway, whether it's a potluck or lunch after church, and give yourself permission to stay forty-five minutes and leave. If you truly can't go, offer another time, because a no without a counteroffer can sound like a no forever.

steps.title: Host badly
steps.body: Invite two people over for soup or takeout on paper plates, and don't clean the whole house first. Scripture's instruction is short, "Practice hospitality" (Romans 12:13), and a table is still one of the best places strangers become friends. If your home isn't possible right now, meet at a diner. Plenty of people are lonelier than they look, and many of them will be glad someone asked first.

steps.title: Tell your pastor you're lonely
steps.body: Church leaders often don't know who's lonely, because lonely people tend to say they're fine. Say it to a pastor or group leader in so many words: *I've been really lonely, and I don't know how to get in here. Can you help me find a place?* A good pastor will be grateful. If your church has no room for that sentence, it may be time to find one that does.

moreHelp.body:
Most of what helps loneliness is ordinary, but sometimes loneliness is more than a pastoral matter. Long loneliness and depression often travel together, and from the inside it can be hard to tell which you're facing. Grief can look like loneliness, and so can old wounds that make closeness feel dangerous. If the loneliness has settled into hopelessness, or you can no longer manage the ordinary things of your life, please talk with a doctor or a counselor as well as your church. That isn't a lack of faith. God works through medicine and good counsel, and while a counselor can't be your community, a good one can help with whatever keeps you from people.

To find someone, start with your doctor, who can check for physical causes and refer you. If you have insurance, your insurer keeps a directory of covered counselors, and a pastor who knows your area often knows which local counselors are good. Whether you choose a Christian counselor or any licensed one, confirm the license with your state's licensing board. If your thoughts turn toward not wanting to live, don't wait for an appointment. Use the lines at the top of this page tonight.
signs: You've had thoughts of not wanting to be alive, or of ending your life. Call or text 988 now, or 911 if you're in danger.
The loneliness has become a hopelessness that hasn't lifted in two weeks or more.
You've stopped sleeping, eating, or getting out of bed the way you used to.
You're drinking or using more to get through the evenings.
Fear or panic keeps you from leaving home or seeing people you want to see.

A spouse or partner controls who you see, or someone at home makes you afraid. Contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline, or 911 if you're in danger. If you're a teenager, tell a teacher or school counselor too.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't need a speech. To a doctor you can say: *I've been very lonely for a long time, and it's affecting my sleep and my mood.* With a counselor's office, describe what's happening in a sentence, then ask a few plain questions. Are you licensed in this state? Do you take my insurance or offer a sliding scale? Have you worked with loneliness, grief, or depression? If your faith matters to you, ask whether they're comfortable with that. If the first counselor isn't a good fit, try another.
moreHelp.cost: Cost shouldn't keep you from help. Many counselors offer sliding-scale fees based on income, so ask. Community mental health centers serve people with little or no insurance, and university training clinics offer supervised counseling at reduced rates. An employee assistance program at work often covers a few free sessions. Many churches keep a benevolence fund, and some will help with counseling costs; ask your pastor. The crisis lines on this page are always free.

helping.body:
Lonely people rarely announce it. They say they're fine, they go quiet, they stop coming, and they turn down invitations, and the turned-down invitation is often less a no than a question about whether anyone will ask twice. So ask twice. What helps most is small and repeated: a standing coffee, a text on a hard anniversary, a saved seat. Bring them into ordinary life, like a weeknight dinner with your kids at the table, and don't make them a project, because people can tell. Paul, a prisoner in Rome, remembered Onesiphorus for exactly this: he "searched diligently until he found me" (2 Timothy 1:17).

If you lead a small group or a church, loneliness is largely a problem of attention. Keep a simple list and notice absence, so that anyone missing for a few weeks gets a call, not to scold them but to say they were missed. Watch for the people churches tend to lose: the widowed once the meals stop, single adults at the holidays, the newly moved, the recently divorced, and caregivers who can't get out. Build smaller rooms inside the big one, where a person can be known by name. Then ask, about every regular attender, the question that matters most: if this person stopped coming for a month, who would call?
say: I've missed you. Can I bring dinner over Thursday?
We do this every Tuesday, and there's a chair for you.
You don't have to be good company. Come anyway.
How are you really doing? I've got time.
Are you thinking about suicide? You can tell me the truth.
dontSay: You just need to put yourself out there.
Jesus should be enough for you.
Enjoy being single while it lasts.
Let me know if you need anything.
helping.next: Before you leave, put the next time on the calendar, because loneliness yields to repetition more than to one good evening. Introduce them to one other person, so the circle doesn't depend on you alone. If you're worried it has turned darker, ask directly whether they're thinking about suicide. Asking doesn't put the idea in anyone's head, and it gives them room to tell the truth. If they say yes, stay with them, call or text 988 together, and bring in a pastor so you aren't carrying this alone. If you learn that a spouse or partner is keeping someone isolated or afraid, treat it as a safety matter first: help them reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline, and don't raise it with the person they fear. If you're a church leader, check what your state's reporting laws require of you, especially if children live in that home.

prayer:
Lord, you said it was not good for us to be alone, and I am alone. I don't fully know how it got this way, and some of it may be my own doing, but tonight it simply hurts. "Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted" (Psalm 25:16).

You know this ache yourself. You asked your friends to stay awake with you, and they slept. You were deserted, and you did not desert us, so I won't be ashamed to bring this to you.

Be near me in the hours that are hardest. Where loneliness has made me bitter, soften me. Where it has made me afraid of people, give me courage for one small step before I feel ready.

You settle the lonely in families. Settle me. Make your church the kind of family that notices, starting with me, so that someone else doesn't sit alone where I have been sitting.

I'm not asking you to take away my need for people. You gave it to me. I'm asking you to meet it, and to hold me in the meantime. Amen.

faq.q: What does the Bible say about loneliness?
faq.a: More than most of us were taught. Genesis calls the man's aloneness not good before sin had entered the world (Genesis 2:18). The Psalms give lonely people words to pray, like "Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted" (Psalm 25:16), and promise that "God settles the lonely in families" (Psalm 68:6). In Gethsemane Jesus asked his friends to keep watch with him, and Paul, in chains, asked Timothy to come before winter (2 Timothy 4:21). Nowhere does Scripture treat God's presence as a reason to stop needing people.

faq.q: If I have Jesus, why do I still feel so alone?
faq.a: Because God made you for himself and for other people, and one doesn't cancel the other. Some of your loneliness is a longing only God can meet. But in the garden the man already had God, and God still said it was not good for him to be alone (Genesis 2:18). In Gethsemane, Jesus was in perfect communion with his Father and still asked his friends to keep watch with him. Needing people isn't a failure of faith. God usually answers loneliness through people, which is why he made a church rather than a scattering of private believers.

faq.q: Why do I feel so alone at church?
faq.a: Often because the part of church you see most is an hour built for worship rather than conversation, and you can attend it faithfully for years without anyone learning your name. That isn't your failure, and it isn't all the New Testament means by church, which it calls a household (Ephesians 2:19). Look for the smaller room inside the big one: a small group, a class, a serving team. Then tell a pastor that you're lonely. Churches often don't know until someone says so.

faq.q: Can you be lonely in your marriage?
faq.a: Yes, and it's among the most painful kinds, because the person meant to know you best is right there. If the loneliness comes from fear, because your spouse controls who you see, threatens you, or hurts you, your safety comes first, before any conversation about the marriage and before any joint counseling. Contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline, or call 911 if you're in danger. When fear isn't part of it, this loneliness can grow from years of drift and busyness, from conflict that was never repaired, or from one spouse carrying far more than the other sees. Tell your spouse plainly and gently, without accusation, and consider seeing a counselor together before it becomes desperate.

faq.q: How do you make friends as an adult?
faq.a: Slowly, and mostly through repetition: seeing the same people regularly somewhere you'd be anyway, like a weekly group, a team, or work done side by side. C. S. Lewis observed in *The Four Loves* that lovers are pictured face to face while friends stand side by side, looking together at something they both care about. That's why serving or building something together often works better than meeting just to connect. Say yes to invitations, make a few of your own, and give it months. Somewhere along the way, someone has to risk saying something true, and you can go first.

faq.q: Nobody checks on me. What should I do?
faq.a: You're not wrong to want someone to. David prayed "no one cares for my soul" (Psalm 142:4) and brought that very sentence to God. It may also help to know that people who don't check on others are often distracted rather than indifferent, or assume someone else has. That doesn't make it hurt less, but one honest message can change more than you'd expect: *I've been having a hard time and could really use a call.* Tell a pastor or group leader too. And if the silence has started to feel like proof that you don't matter, please reach someone tonight through the lines at the top of this page.

slots.note: James came to faith from atheism. If he chooses, he could add a few sentences in his own words on what it was like to come into the church from outside: whether it felt like a household or an audience, and who made room for him. The section stands without it.
Psalm 68:5 calls God a father of the fatherless. James was raised without a father; he could add a sentence to the Psalm 68 reading on what that line has meant to him, only if he wants to.

As a pastor and the founder of the Pastors Connection Network, James could add, in his own words, what he has seen help lonely pastors and whether PCN is a place a lonely pastor can turn. The page makes no claim about PCN's purpose.

sources.claim: You do not need to be in suicidal crisis to contact 988; the reasons people reach out include emotional distress and loneliness.
